# Tides

Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea. On most coasts the tide comes in twice a day [c-fbebef7001b9]. The harbour's own tables are the first thing to read [s-kb-0123456789abcdef].

## Key terms

- **Spring tide**: the higher tide near a new or full moon [c-0a1b2c3d4e5f].
- **Tide table**: a published list of the times of high and low water [s-local-tides-md-3277c799].

## Contents

- [Why twice a day](#why-twice-a-day)
- [Spring and neap tides](#spring-and-neap-tides)

## Why twice a day

The moon pulls the sea towards it, and the turning earth carries each coast through two bulges of water a day [c-fbebef7001b9, s-local-tides-md-3277c799].

> The tide comes in twice a day.

A scout's finding in this workspace gives the same reason and marks it open [f-fedcba9876543210].

### What the tables add

The almanac's table gives the times of high water for each harbour [c-5d6e7f809a1b].

## Spring and neap tides

Spring tides are higher than usual and come near a new or full moon [c-0a1b2c3d4e5f ● validated]. Whether the harbour's ledger recorded them is disputed [c-77aa88bb99cc].

For the lamps that mark the harbour mouth at high water, see [Lighthouse lamps](page:lighthouse-lamps), or go back to [why twice a day](#why-twice-a-day).

## Start here

1. Read the harbour's tide table first [s-local-tides-md-3277c799].
2. Then the claim that tides come twice a day [c-fbebef7001b9].
3. Then the scout's finding on why [f-fedcba9876543210].

## See also

- [Lighthouse lamps](page:lighthouse-lamps)

## Open questions

- From the research record: no source on the list says how tides differ in the harbour's inner basin.

Read the harbour's own tables before putting to sea.
